intro: Paris is best experienced in layers: its icons at opening time, its smaller museums and markets by day, then long walks and dinner as the city begins to glow.

places.name: Eiffel Tower
places.why_go: The city’s defining silhouette earns its reputation with remarkable views and a thrilling sense of scale from the Champ de Mars.
places.description: The Eiffel Tower is at its best when you plan around the crowds rather than treating it as a spontaneous stop. The lift ride and summit panorama reveal Paris’s geography—the Seine, Trocadéro, Montmartre, and the dense Haussmann streets—while the lower levels offer a less frantic perspective. Pair it with an early walk on the Champ de Mars or a sunset view from Trocadéro, but expect security screening and queues.
places.how_to_get_there: Use Bir-Hakeim on Metro Line 6, École Militaire on Line 8, or Champ de Mars–Tour Eiffel on RER C, then walk to the entrance selected on your ticket.
places.cost: Tickets vary significantly by level and stairs versus lift; expect paid entry and check the official site for current prices.
places.booking_tip: Book official timed tickets as soon as dates open, particularly for summit access. Arrive ahead of your slot for security and avoid unofficial resellers.

places.name: Louvre Museum
places.why_go: A former royal palace containing masterpieces from antiquity to the nineteenth century, far richer than its famous pyramid photo suggests.
places.description: The Louvre can overwhelm if approached as a box-ticking marathon, so choose two or three wings: perhaps Egyptian antiquities, the French apartments, and the Italian paintings. The Mona Lisa is an experience in crowd management, but the museum’s real pleasure lies in quieter rooms, monumental staircases, and the palace itself. A short, deliberate visit is more rewarding than an exhausted full-day attempt.
places.how_to_get_there: Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre is served by Metro Lines 1 and 7; use the entrance indicated by your timed reservation.
places.cost: Adult admission is paid and prices can change; consult the official Louvre ticket page, including eligibility for free entry.
places.booking_tip: A timed reservation is generally required even when admission is free. Choose the first entry or a late slot and confirm which entrances are open.

places.name: Montmartre and Sacré-Cœur
places.why_go: Hilltop Paris delivers sweeping views, the white-domed basilica, village lanes, and a dash of bohemian history.
places.description: Montmartre rewards an early or late visit, when you can climb beyond the souvenir stalls into quieter streets around Place des Abbesses and the vineyards. Sacré-Cœur’s interior is free to enter, and the steps outside create one of the city’s broadest views. The neighborhood is steep and busy, so wander a few blocks away from Place du Tertre to find its more convincing small-scale character.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 2 to Anvers or Line 12 to Abbesses, then walk uphill; the Montmartre funicular is useful with a valid transit ticket.
places.cost: The basilica is free; the dome and funicular have separate conditions or fares. Check current access before visiting.
places.booking_tip: No booking is needed for the basilica. Arrive early for calmer steps and be alert to pickpocketing and aggressive souvenir sellers in crowded approaches.

places.name: Musée d’Orsay
places.why_go: Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces shine inside an extraordinary former railway station.
places.description: Orsay’s compact story of art from 1848 to 1914 makes it one of Paris’s most satisfying museums. Work upward through paintings, decorative arts, and sculpture, saving the top-floor Impressionist rooms and station clock view for later. Monet, Degas, Renoir, Cézanne, Van Gogh, and Gauguin are all here in real depth, while the Beaux-Arts architecture makes the route feel cinematic.
places.how_to_get_there: Use Solférino on Metro Line 12 or Musée d’Orsay on RER C; it is also an easy Seine walk from the Louvre or Saint-Germain.
places.cost: Standard admission is paid, commonly in the high-teens of euros; check official rates, reduced tickets, and free-entry policies.
places.booking_tip: Reserve a timed ticket in high season. A Thursday evening opening can be less crowded, but confirm current hours first.

places.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
places.why_go: The restored Gothic cathedral remains the spiritual and geographic heart of historic Paris.
places.description: Notre-Dame’s facade, flying buttresses, and position on the Île de la Cité make it essential even for visitors not attending a service. After the 2019 fire and subsequent restoration, access arrangements, visitor flows, and reservations may evolve, so treat current official information as decisive. Combine it with a slow circuit of the island, including riverside views and the nearby flower market.
places.how_to_get_there: Cité on Metro Line 4 is nearby; Saint-Michel–Notre-Dame connects RER B/C and Metro Line 4 on the Left Bank side.
places.cost: The cathedral’s general visitor access is typically free, though specific tours, towers, or exhibitions may have separate rules.
places.booking_tip: Check the official cathedral website shortly before your visit for current entry procedures, service times, and any required free reservation.

places.name: Sainte-Chapelle
places.why_go: A jewel-box Gothic chapel where towering stained glass turns daylight into a full-room spectacle.
places.description: Sainte-Chapelle is small enough to visit in under an hour but visually intense enough to anchor an afternoon on the Île de la Cité. The upper chapel’s fifteenth-century glass surrounds you with biblical stories, so take a few minutes to let your eyes adjust rather than rushing through. Security is similar to a courthouse setting because it sits within the former Palais de la Cité complex.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 4 to Cité or Saint-Michel–Notre-Dame, then walk across the island to Boulevard du Palais.
places.cost: Paid admission is usual, with combined monument tickets sometimes available; verify the current official rate.
places.booking_tip: Reserve a timed entry online and arrive early for security screening. Sunny days bring out the glass most vividly, though crowds can be heavier.

places.name: Arc de Triomphe
places.why_go: Climb above the Champs-Élysées for a powerful view of Paris’s radiating avenues and the Eiffel Tower beyond.
places.description: The Arc’s rooftop offers a much clearer sense of Parisian urban planning than you get from street level: twelve avenues fan around the Étoile in an enormous traffic circle. Inside, the history of the monument and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier add gravity to the panorama. Use the underground pedestrian passage—never attempt to cross the roundabout on foot.
places.how_to_get_there: Charles de Gaulle–Étoile is served by Metro Lines 1, 2, and 6 and RER A; follow signs to the pedestrian underpass.
places.cost: Rooftop access is paid, generally around the mid-teens of euros; grounds-level viewing is free.
places.booking_tip: Book ahead in peak periods and check last-entry times. Sunset slots are popular, so allow time for stairs and security.

places.name: Luxembourg Gardens
places.why_go: Formal lawns, fountains, chestnut shade, and Left Bank calm make this Paris’s most gracious everyday park.
places.description: The Luxembourg Gardens are built for taking a pause: choose a green chair by the central basin, watch children sail model boats, then explore the Medici Fountain and tree-lined edges. It feels both stately and lived-in, with runners, students, and chess players sharing the grounds. The garden is a natural breather between Saint-Germain, the Panthéon, and the Latin Quarter.
places.how_to_get_there: Luxembourg station on RER B is closest; Odéon (Metro Lines 4 and 10) is a ten-minute walk.
places.cost: Entry is free. Some activities, exhibitions, or refreshments cost extra.
places.booking_tip: No booking needed. Check posted seasonal opening hours, as gates close earlier in winter and some lawns may be restricted.

places.name: Le Marais
places.why_go: A historic district of mansions, fashion, Jewish heritage, galleries, and one of Paris’s loveliest squares.
places.description: Le Marais holds several different Parises within a compact walking area: aristocratic hôtels particuliers, the Jewish quarter around Rue des Rosiers, contemporary design shops, and the arcades of Place des Vosges. Skip a strict itinerary and meander between small streets, pausing at a museum or bakery that genuinely appeals. It is exceptionally popular, but an early weekday visit reveals more of its residential texture.
places.how_to_get_there: Saint-Paul on Metro Line 1 and Chemin Vert on Line 8 are useful starting points; many parts are best explored on foot.
places.cost: Free to wander; museums, cafés, and shopping vary from modest to expensive.
places.booking_tip: No booking is required for the neighborhood. Reserve well-known restaurants and note that some independent shops observe limited Sunday or Monday hours.

places.name: Centre Pompidou
places.why_go: Its inside-out architecture and formidable modern-art collection make it a bold contrast to Paris’s classical landmarks.
places.description: The Pompidou is an art destination and an urban balcony at once: the external escalator frames views over rooftops while the galleries move through modern and contemporary movements in depth. Exhibition programs and building access can change during renovation phases, so verify the current status before relying on a visit. If open, the plaza outside is as much part of the experience as the collection.
places.how_to_get_there: Rambuteau on Metro Line 11 is closest; Hôtel de Ville (Lines 1 and 11) and Châtelet are walkable alternatives.
places.cost: Collection and exhibition tickets are normally paid; prices and access may change with programming or renovation work.
places.booking_tip: Check the official website before travel for opening status and book timed tickets for major exhibitions.

places.name: Canal Saint-Martin
places.why_go: Tree-lined water, iron footbridges, and relaxed cafés offer a slower, more local-feeling Paris walk.
places.description: Follow the canal north from République to watch boats navigate locks and to see a side of Paris built around neighborhood routines instead of monuments. The banks invite a picnic or coffee break, though local rules and seasonal conditions can affect where you may sit or drink. Detour into the streets around Rue de Marseille and Rue des Vinaigriers for independent shops and casual food.
places.how_to_get_there: République is served by Metro Lines 3, 5, 8, 9, and 11; Jacques Bonsergent on Line 5 is another convenient start.
places.cost: Free to walk; canal cruises and cafés are optional paid extras.
places.booking_tip: No booking needed for the promenade. Go in daylight, respect residential noise, and reserve nearby restaurants on warm weekend evenings.

places.name: Marché des Enfants Rouges
places.why_go: Paris’s oldest covered market is a compact, delicious stop for market stalls and international lunch counters.
places.description: Tucked into the Marais, this historic market is a practical alternative to a formal restaurant lunch. Its counters range from French produce and charcuterie to Japanese, North African, and Italian-inspired dishes, so it works well for groups with different appetites. Seating is limited and turnover is quick; browse first, then choose a stall with a manageable line.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 8 to Filles du Calvaire or Line 3 to Temple, then walk a few minutes.
places.cost: Entry is free; expect roughly €10–€25 for a prepared lunch, depending on stall and drinks.
places.booking_tip: No reservation is typical. Confirm opening days and hours, as market schedules and individual stalls can vary.

places.name: Panthéon
places.why_go: A neoclassical monument of national memory with Foucault’s pendulum and a powerful Latin Quarter setting.
places.description: Originally conceived as a church, the Panthéon became a mausoleum for figures central to French history and culture, including Voltaire, Victor Hugo, Marie Curie, and Joséphine Baker. Its cavernous interior rewards a slow look at the murals and crypt, while the dome view—when open—adds a lesser-known Paris panorama. It combines easily with the Sorbonne area and Rue Mouffetard.
places.how_to_get_there: Cardinal Lemoine on Metro Line 10 or Luxembourg on RER B are both about a ten-minute walk.
places.cost: Admission is paid for most adult visitors, usually in the mid-teens of euros; confirm current official pricing and dome access.
places.booking_tip: Prebooking is helpful in summer and school holidays. Check the calendar for ceremonies or weather-related dome closures.

places.name: Palais Garnier
places.why_go: A lavish opera house where marble staircases, gilding, and Chagall’s ceiling turn an interior visit into theater.
places.description: Palais Garnier is worth visiting even without an opera ticket: the Grand Staircase, auditorium, and ornate foyers show off the theatrical excess of Second Empire Paris. Self-guided access may be limited around rehearsals and performances, so keep expectations flexible. For a full evening, pair an interior tour with a performance at Garnier or the modern Opéra Bastille, depending on the season.
places.how_to_get_there: Opéra station is served by Metro Lines 3, 7, and 8; Auber on RER A is nearby.
places.cost: Self-guided visits and performances are paid separately, with performance pricing varying widely by seat and production.
places.booking_tip: Reserve tours or performance tickets through official channels. Verify same-day visitor access because rehearsals can close parts of the building.

places.name: Seine River Walk
places.why_go: A simple riverside walk stitches together Paris’s landmarks, bridges, bookstalls, and its most romantic changing light.
places.description: Walk a chosen stretch rather than trying to cover the whole river: the Left Bank between Musée d’Orsay and Notre-Dame is rich in views, while the section around Pont Alexandre III and the Eiffel Tower feels grander. Browse the green bouquiniste boxes, watch boats pass, and cross a bridge whenever a street or neighborhood draws you in. River levels, works, and event security can occasionally close embankments.
places.how_to_get_there: Start at any central river-adjacent station, such as Pont Neuf (Line 7), Saint-Michel (Line 4), or Invalides (Lines 8 and 13, RER C).
places.cost: Free to walk. Sightseeing cruises are optional and range in price; compare operators and departure times before booking.
places.booking_tip: No reservation is needed for the walk. Wear comfortable shoes, check the weather, and use well-lit central routes after dark.
